title: The friendship paradox
text: Social scientists have noticed a curious pattern: on average, your friends have more friends than you {{1}}. This 'friendship paradox' is not an insult {{2}} at your social life but simple mathematics. Popular people appear in more people's lists of friends, so when you sample friends randomly, you {{3}} up oversampling popular people. The same logic {{4}} why your sexual partners' partners seem busier, why co-authors have more publications than you, and why the people you follow online seem to lead richer lives. Researchers {{5}} that the effect can distort our judgement: we compare ourselves with an unusually glittering sample of humanity and find ourselves {{6}}. The paradox even has practical {{7}}: during a flu outbreak, checking the friends of randomly chosen people detects epidemics weeks earlier, because well-connected individuals {{8}} infections first. Sometimes being strictly average comes at a hidden cost.

gaps.explanation: 'more friends than you do' — do substitutes for the verb.
'aimed at' — the fixed participle; intended and addressed take 'for' and 'to'.
'end up + -ing' = eventually be in a state; take up + -ing means start as an activity, and turn up and come up mean arrive and arise.
'researchers argue' = claim a position; announce is for formal public news, notify needs a person as object, and confess implies admitting wrongdoing.
'find ourselves lacking' = discover we are not enough; missing and absent describe things that are not present, and misplaced is for objects.
'practical uses' — how it can be applied; profits, earnings and expenses are money words that do not follow 'practical'.
'catch infections' — the collocation for getting a disease.
